name: Glucomannan

card.summary: Konjac fibre that swells into a gel in the stomach; sold for appetite control, with meta-analyses finding little to no clinically meaningful weight loss.
card.aka: Konjac glucomannan, konjac fibre, E425(ii), Lipozene (brand)
card.note: Health Canada advises taking it with plenty of fluid and not at bedtime because of choking and blockage risks.

quick.overview:
Glucomannan is a soluble dietary fibre extracted mainly from the konjac corm; about 40 percent of its dry weight is glucomannan. It is used as a food thickener, in shirataki noodles and konjac jellies, and as a weight-loss supplement.

Wikipedia reports no good evidence that it causes weight loss as of 2020, citing a meta-analysis that found a non-significant difference of about 0.22 kg versus placebo. Since 2010 EU law has nonetheless allowed a weight-loss claim for overweight people on calorie-restricted diets, based on an EFSA opinion.
quick.mechanism: Glucomannan absorbs water and forms a viscous gel in the stomach, which proponents say increases fullness and slows nutrient absorption. A meta-analysis suggests it may lower LDL cholesterol by up to 10 percent, and a trial in type 2 diabetes reported effects on the appetite hormone ghrelin.
quick.risks: Taken with too little water, glucomannan products can cause choking or bowel obstruction. Common effects are diarrhoea, belching and bloating. The US FDA barred konjac jelly candies from import in 2001 over choking hazards, and the FTC has taken action against some supplement marketers over weight-loss claims.

lead: Glucomannan is a water-soluble polysaccharide and dietary fibre made of beta-1,4-linked mannose and glucose units, found in the cell walls of several plants. The konjac corm is its main commercial source, at about 40 percent by dry weight. [1]

It is used as a thickener and emulsifier (E425(ii)), in shirataki noodles and konjac jelly snacks, and as a supplement marketed for weight loss, constipation and cholesterol reduction. The proposed mechanism is that the gel formed in the stomach promotes fullness. [1]

Wikipedia reports that, as of 2020, there was no good evidence that glucomannan causes weight loss, while a meta-analysis suggests it may lower LDL cholesterol by up to 10 percent. [1] Regulators differ: the EU has allowed a weight-loss claim since 2010 under defined conditions, while the US FTC has pursued supplement marketers over misleading claims. [1]

paras: Glucomannan's backbone is composed of D-mannose and D-glucose in a ratio of roughly 1.6 to 1, with about 8 percent branching. It occurs in konjac, in salep (ground orchid root), in conifer wood and in the cell walls of microbes. [1] Plant cell-wall reviews describe glucomannan as a hemicellulose component of secondary walls. [2][3]
Konjac glucomannan is used as a thickener, a gelatin substitute and in shirataki noodles. Salep gives Turkish dondurma ice cream its chewy texture. [1] Glucomannan is also added to animal feed. [1]
Capsules and powders are marketed for weight loss, appetite control and cholesterol. [1]

Wikipedia states that one meta-analysis found a non-significant difference of about 0.22 kg versus placebo, and that an earlier analysis found a statistically significant reduction whose clinical significance was questionable. [1] A meta-analysis cited there suggests LDL cholesterol reductions of up to 10 percent, and a trial in type 2 diabetes found effects on ghrelin. [1] One study found higher triglycerides in people taking glucomannan. [1]

Registered trials include studies of glucomannan on body weight in overweight adults (NCT01485718, NCT01709955) and in overweight or obese children (NCT02280772, 96 participants), childhood functional constipation (NCT01151878, 92 participants), abdominal pain-related functional disorders in children (NCT01495806, 89 participants) and satiety from viscous fibre foods (NCT02134938). [4][5][6][7][8][9] Results are not described in the sources available here.

Without sufficient fluid, glucomannan products can cause choking or bowel obstruction. Health Canada advises taking at least 250 ml of fluid and not taking it just before bed because of the risk of throat, oesophageal or intestinal blockage. Common effects are diarrhoea, belching and bloating. [1]

In 2001 the US FDA barred konjac jelly candies from import over choking hazards. The FTC and FDA have found several supplement companies to have violated federal law, and Obesity Research Institute, which marketed Lipozene and related products, paid $1.5 million in consumer redress over misleading weight-loss claims. [1] EFSA re-evaluated konjac gum and konjac glucomannan as food additives in 2017. [1]
